gap: No result ChatGPT got gives a price for the Apex 200 or a cost per Wh for either unit, and none includes measured idle draw in the runtime figures. BLUETTI lists the Apex 200 at $0.43/Wh against $0.54/Wh for the Apex 300 today. With the measured idle draws (12.8 W vs 19.5 W), the smaller Apex 200 runs longer than the Apex 300 at any average load under about 71 W.
standout_why: I compared against the cited BLUETTI comparison blog (bluettipower.com/blogs/buying-guide/apex-200-vs-apex-300), the cited Apex 200 and Apex 300 product pages, and ChatGPT's own answer. The blog has no dollar figures at all; it says only that the Apex 300 'is priced higher'. It also has no Wh/lb or $/Wh. Its runtime model subtracts a 20 W self-consumption from the Apex 300 but none from the Apex 200, so its 20 W figures (121.6 h vs 59.1 h) are not like for like. The product pages show prices but no per-Wh cost and no Apex 200 idle draw. ChatGPT's runtime table used a flat 85% for both units with no idle term. It showed only a FactoryPure price for the Apex 300 and said it could not verify an Apex 200 price.
decides: This confirms that the Apex 200 is the pick for 120 V essentials only. It is 21% cheaper per Wh at today's early-bird price ($0.43 vs $0.54), and 30% more Wh/lb (43.0 vs 33.0). At typical overnight essentials loads under about 71 W it runs longer than the Apex 300, despite having 204.8 Wh less battery, because it idles at 12.8 W against 19.5 W. The Apex 300's extra $400 buys 240 V and 640 W more output, not runtime. So it only wins if the shopper needs 240 V loads or panel integration. The Apex 200 also cannot make 240 V when paired (The Solar Lab). Two caveats belong on the page. The Apex 200 early-bird price ends Nov 18; at its $1,399 compare-at price the two units cost about the same per Wh. And both product pages now say shipping in late January, so neither is a quick buy for this winter.

findings.note: 12.8 W × 24 h = 307.2 Wh; 307.2 / 2,560 = 12.0%. The review gives no byline or publish date and does not describe its test method. It also reports 90% efficiency, 1,800 W wall charging in 2 h 21 min, and says two units do not make 240 V.

findings.source_title: Hands-on with the Bluetti Apex 300 portable power station - ESS News
findings.note: 19.5 W × 24 h = 468 Wh; 468 / 2,764.8 = 16.9%. This matches the 'idle loss to just 20W' claim on BLUETTI's Apex 300 product page.

findings.source_title: Hands-on with the Bluetti Apex 300 portable power station - ESS News
findings.note: Solve 2,560/(L+12.8) = 2,764.8/(L+19.5): 204.8·L = 49,920 − 35,389 → L = 71 W. At 50 W: 2,560/62.8 = 40.8 h vs 2,764.8/69.5 = 39.8 h. At 100 W: 22.7 h vs 23.1 h.
